newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: WWII row costs SBC "handful" of clients.
newsitem.headline: WWII row costs SBC "handful" of clients.

text.p: Swiss Bank Corp, one of the three biggest Swiss banks, said on Wednesday it had lost a handful of customers due to controversy over dormant accounts that victims of the Holocaust left in neutral Switzerland.
But SBC executives said the bank had not lost any clients from its lucrative and growing business for institutional investors in North America, where the row has been heavily covered by the media.

Chief executive Marcel Ospel said some individual customers had pulled out either because Swiss banks are accused of hoarding Holocaust accounts or in protest at a memorial fund the big banks have paid into for survivors of Nazi genocide.
"It is absolutely within limits. We are talking about a handful of customer relationships world-wide," Ospel told a news conference on the bank's 1996 financial results.

World Jewish groups have accused Swiss banks of deliberately sitting on billions of dollars in wealth left by Jews and other Holocaust victims, part of a wider debate over the country's role as a financial centre while World War Two raged around it.
The banks deny any wrongdoing and last May set up an independent commission with major Jewish groups to scour bank records for any unreported accounts left by Nazi victims.

The head of SBC's profitable and growing institutional investment division SBC Brinson, Gary Brinson, said he had lost no customers in the United States, which provides 68 percent of the division's institutional client assets.

"There is an appropriate level of concern among some of our clients in the United States. But to date none of them have taken action which would result in the termination or loss of mandates," Brinson told the SBC group annual news conference.

Brinson suggested the threat of customer reprisals was receding since Swiss banks and the government took dramatic steps in the past month to appease critics, including setting up the Holocaust memorial fund of 265 million Swiss francs ($179.5 million) paid by commercial banks, Swiss businesses and the central bank.
"I think the general feeling today is that the response that is being provided by both the Swiss banks and by the government is leading to a better path of communication and understanding," he said.

Ospel said SBC had found 11.4 million Swiss francs from 290 customers in a search launched in 1995 by members of the Swiss Bankers Association for dormant accounts that may have been left by customers murdered in the Holocaust.
The SBC find is part of a total of about 40 million Swiss francs reported by all banks based on a search for assets deposited before 1945 and whose owners had made no contact for at least 10 years.
Credit Suisse Group has located around 14.9 million francs in such accounts, and Union Bank of Switzerland some 10 million. ($ = 1.476 Swiss Francs)
